## Two different restriction mechanisms

Restricted regression constrains the coefficients estimated for predictions:
`learner_params = list(restricted = list(rules = model_rules))`.
Generic edit restrictions constrain completed numeric imputation values:
`edit_rules = final_rules`. Both arguments take `validate::validator()` objects.
They are independent and are never merged. The restricted learner still
requires its own model rules and retains its `uncert = "none"` override.

The generic mechanism works with numeric predictions from ranger, xgboost,
tabicl2, regularized, robust, gam, robgam, restricted, and registered numeric
learners. One projection follows each complete sweep, after stochastic draws
and rounding, before convergence and chain statistics. Adjusted values feed
into the next sweep. Projection is joint across target variables and methods.

## A structural business-survey example

The bundled `lse_synthetic` dataset and `lse_synthetic_rules` provide a wider
structural business-survey example. Here we take its continuous turnover
components and impose a compact subset of linear edits. Convert integer
storage explicitly when the variables are intended to represent continuous
amounts. Discrete employee counts are outside this continuous optimizer.

```{r example-data}
library(VIM)
data(lse_synthetic, package = "VIM")
cols <- c("turnover_total", "turnover_domestic", "turnover_exports", "onace_section")
business <- lse_synthetic[seq_len(100), cols]
business[cols[1:3]] <- lapply(business[cols[1:3]], as.numeric)
business$turnover_total[1:10] <- NA_real_
business$turnover_domestic[5:15] <- NA_real_
business$turnover_exports[8:18] <- NA_real_
final_rules <- validate::validator(
  accounting = turnover_total == turnover_domestic + turnover_exports,
  turnover_total >= 0,
  turnover_domestic >= 0,
  turnover_exports >= 0
)
```

Rules may use fixed columns excluded by `considered_variables`; these columns
are read from the original input and do not become model predictors.
A missing fixed rule value raises an error. Observed cells remain fixed, so an
observed record violating an edit cannot be repaired by changing its observations.

## Ranger and XGBoost

```{r ranger}
rf <- vimpute(business, method = "ranger", edit_rules = final_rules,
  learner_params = list(ranger = list(num.trees = 100L)),
  sequential = FALSE, uncert = "none", seed = 1)
```

```{r xgboost}
boost <- vimpute(business, method = "xgboost", edit_rules = final_rules,
  learner_params = list(xgboost = list(nrounds = 30L)),
  sequential = TRUE, nseq = 3L, uncert = "none", seed = 1)
```

## TabICL and mixed methods

TabICL needs the optional Python environment described in `tabiclImpute()`.
The example is displayed rather than run during package builds, so it cannot
download checkpoints. Its model is independent of the ECOS projection.

```{r tabicl}
tab <- vimpute(business, method = "tabicl2", edit_rules = final_rules,
  learner_params = list(tabicl2 = list(finetune = FALSE, device = "cpu")),
  sequential = FALSE, uncert = "none", seed = 1)
```

The next example mixes coefficient-restricted regression, Ranger and TabICL.
The accounting identity is imposed once on the joint completed record after
all three models produce their imputations.

```{r mixed}
model_rules <- validate::validator(turnover_total >= 0)
mixed <- vimpute(business,
  method = list(turnover_total = "restricted", turnover_domestic = "ranger",
                turnover_exports = "tabicl2"),
  learner_params = list(
    turnover_total = list(rules = model_rules),
    turnover_domestic = list(num.trees = 100L),
    turnover_exports = list(device = "cpu", finetune = FALSE)),
  edit_rules = final_rules,
  edit_control = vimpute_edit_control(weights = "scaled"),
  sequential = TRUE, nseq = 3L, uncert = "none", seed = 1)
```

## Two validators can deliberately disagree

The coefficient stage below predicts at least four in the missing row.
The generic stage independently restricts that row to at most three. It changes
that prediction to three. Only the generic validator is guaranteed for the
final output: parameter-stage rules not included there may cease to hold.

```{r independent-rules}
d <- data.frame(y = c(1, 2, NA_real_), x = c(1, 2, 3))
model_rules <- validate::validator(y >= 4)
final_rules <- validate::validator(if (x > 2) y <= 3)
result <- vimpute(d, method = "restricted",
  learner_params = list(restricted = list(rules = model_rules,
    save_optimization_problem = TRUE)),
  edit_rules = final_rules,
  edit_control = list(save_optimization_problem = TRUE),
  sequential = FALSE, uncert = "none")
```

## Examples carried over from restricted regression

The following examples reproduce the interval, conditional, formula and robust
regression scenarios from the restricted regression vignette. Each passes the
numeric rules explicitly to both `learner_params` and `edit_rules`: the first
constrains the restricted model, and the second checks the completed records
and projects any remaining violations. All observed records in these examples
satisfy the final edits. To run only the original coefficient restrictions,
omit `edit_rules`.

These examples require the optional restricted-regression dependencies,
including `validate`, `ECOSolveR` and the mlr3 stack. Like the other examples in
this vignette, they are displayed without execution during package builds.

## Interval Rules

Restricted regression is most natural when variables have row-wise lower and
upper bounds. In this example `amount` is imputed while every completed value
must remain between its corresponding `lower` and `upper` columns.

```{r interval-rules, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
set.seed(42)
n <- 100L

bounded_data <- data.frame(
  x1 = stats::runif(n, 0, 10),
  x2 = stats::runif(n, -2, 2)
)
bounded_data$amount <- 20 + 1.5 * bounded_data$x1 - 0.75 * bounded_data$x2
bounded_data$lower <- bounded_data$amount - 0.5
bounded_data$upper <- bounded_data$amount + 0.5
bounded_data <- bounded_data[, c("amount", "x1", "x2", "lower", "upper")]

missing_idx <- sample.int(n, 20L)
bounded_missing <- bounded_data
bounded_missing$amount[missing_idx] <- NA_real_

bounded_rules <- validate::validator(
  amount >= lower,
  amount <= upper,
  amount >= 0,
  lower <= upper
)

bounded_imp <- vimpute(
  bounded_missing,
  method = list(amount = "restricted"),
  pmm = FALSE,
  sequential = FALSE,
  edit_rules = bounded_rules,
  learner_params = list(amount = list(rules = bounded_rules))
)

head(bounded_imp[bounded_imp$amount_imp, c("amount", "lower", "upper")])
```

```{r interval-check}
completed <- as.data.frame(bounded_imp)[, names(bounded_data), drop = FALSE]

sum(bounded_imp$amount_imp)
all(validate::values(validate::confront(completed, bounded_rules)))
```

## Categorical and conditional rules

Rules can also involve categorical predictors and conditional logic. The
restricted learner uses the edit rules only to constrain the imputed target; the
remaining columns can be numeric or categorical predictors.

```{r conditional-rules, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
categorical_data <- bounded_missing
categorical_data$c1 <- factor(rep(c("A", "B", "C"), length.out = n))
categorical_data$c2 <- factor(rep(c("B", "C", "A"), length.out = n))
categorical_data$c3 <- factor(rep(c("C", "A", "B"), length.out = n))

conditional_rules <- validate::validator(
  amount >= lower,
  amount <= upper,
  amount >= 0,
  lower <= upper,
  (c1 == "A") + (c2 == "A") + (c3 == "A") <= 2,
  if (c1 == "A") amount >= 2
)

# The categorical count rule concerns only observed, fixed predictors.
fixed_category_rules <- validate::validator(
  (c1 == "A") + (c2 == "A") + (c3 == "A") <= 2
)
stopifnot(all(validate::values(validate::confront(
  categorical_data, fixed_category_rules
))))
conditional_final_rules <- validate::validator(
  amount >= lower,
  amount <= upper,
  amount >= 0,
  lower <= upper,
  if (c1 == "A") amount >= 2
)

categorical_imp <- vimpute(
  categorical_data,
  method = list(amount = "restricted"),
  pmm = FALSE,
  sequential = FALSE,
  edit_rules = conditional_final_rules,
  learner_params = list(amount = list(rules = conditional_rules))
)

all(validate::values(validate::confront(categorical_imp, conditional_rules)))
```

The original categorical count rule remains in the restricted learner's
validator. Its sum of categorical comparisons is not supported by the generic
linear parser, so we check it separately before imputation. The final projector
uses the numeric bounds and the conditional rule, whose condition depends on
an observed categorical value.

## Formula Control

`formula` can be used with `method = "restricted"` to choose the predictors in
the regression model while the edit rules still constrain the final
predictions. The left-hand side must be the untransformed target variable.

```{r formula-control, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
n_formula <- 80L
formula_data <- data.frame(
  y = 10 + 2 * seq_len(n_formula),
  x_signal = seq_len(n_formula),
  x_noise = 10 + 2 * seq_len(n_formula),
  lower = 0,
  upper = 200
)

formula_missing_idx <- c(12L, 24L, 36L)
expected_y <- formula_data$y[formula_missing_idx]
formula_data$y[formula_missing_idx] <- NA_real_
formula_data$x_noise[formula_missing_idx] <- -1000

formula_rules <- validate::validator(y >= lower, y <= upper, lower <= upper)

formula_imp <- vimpute(
  formula_data,
  method = list(y = "restricted"),
  formula = list(y = y ~ x_signal),
  pmm = FALSE,
  sequential = FALSE,
  edit_rules = formula_rules,
  learner_params = list(y = list(rules = formula_rules))
)

formula_imp[formula_missing_idx, c("y", "x_signal", "x_noise", "y_imp")]
max(abs(formula_imp$y[formula_missing_idx] - expected_y))
```

## Robust Restricted Regression

Set `robust = TRUE` to use a Huber loss instead of ordinary least squares. This
is helpful when the observed data contain influential outliers but the final
imputed values must still obey the edit rules.

```{r robust-restricted, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
robust_rules <- validate::validator(y >= 0)

outlier_data <- data.frame(
  x = 0:21,
  y = 1 + 2 * (0:21)
)
outlier_data$y[21L] <- 500
outlier_data$y[22L] <- NA_real_

ordinary_imp <- vimpute(
  outlier_data,
  method = list(y = "restricted"),
  formula = list(y = y ~ x),
  pmm = FALSE,
  sequential = FALSE,
  edit_rules = robust_rules,
  learner_params = list(y = list(rules = robust_rules))
)

robust_imp <- vimpute(
  outlier_data,
  method = list(y = "restricted"),
  formula = list(y = y ~ x),
  pmm = FALSE,
  sequential = FALSE,
  edit_rules = robust_rules,
  learner_params = list(y = list(
    rules = robust_rules,
    robust = TRUE,
    huber_k = 1.345
  ))
)

c(
  ordinary = ordinary_imp$y[22L],
  robust = robust_imp$y[22L],
  expected_without_outlier = 43
)
```

## Weighted record-level optimization

For each record, let $M$ contain eligible imputed numeric cells, and
$\hat x_M$ the values already written by the imputation engine. After substituting
fixed values in all active rules, solve

$$\min_{x_M}\;\frac12(x_M-\hat x_M)^T W(x_M-\hat x_M),
\qquad A x_M \le b,\quad E x_M=f.$$

ECOS solves the equivalent norm epigraph in centered coordinates
$z=\sqrt{W}(x_M-\hat x_M)$. Matrix dimensions depend on the number of adjusted
variables in one record, not on the total number of missing cells. Feasible
predictions are returned exactly without calling the solver. Solver termination,
finite values and absolute rule residuals are checked before application; final
output is checked again after normal result construction.

`weights = "equal"` measures absolute distances in input units. The default
`"scaled"` uses inverse squared observed scales (MAD, IQR/1.349, SD, then one).
Constant or nearly constant variables use one; extreme scales are bounded to
avoid overflow. These scales do not estimate predictive uncertainty. Cells
selected by `makeNA` do not contribute to observed scales. A named positive
weight vector must cover every eligible numeric variable referenced by the edits.

```{r control}
control <- vimpute_edit_control(
  weights = c(turnover_total = 1, turnover_domestic = 2, turnover_exports = 2),
  tolerance = 1e-6, on_infeasible = "error",
  save_optimization_problem = TRUE
)
```

## Stochastic and multiple imputation

For other learners, bootstrap, PMM, residual sampling and normal-error draws
retain their normal behavior before projection. Projected PMM values can move
away from their donors. Each multiple-imputation dataset is projected separately.
`vim_complete()` returns completed data with that run's edit diagnostics.

```{r multiple-imputation}
mi <- vimpute(business, method = "ranger", edit_rules = validate::validator(
    turnover_total == turnover_domestic + turnover_exports,
    turnover_domestic >= 0, turnover_exports >= 0),
  m = 5L, boot = TRUE, uncert = "normalerror", seed = 7)
completed <- vim_complete(mi, 1)
attr(completed, "edit_diagnostics")
```

Deterministic projection can reduce between-imputation variance and change the
joint distribution. Projection of stochastic imputations is not, by itself, a
justification for theoretically proper multiple imputation.

## Diagnostics

`attr(result, "edit_diagnostics")` reports unique records ever adjusted,
unique variables adjusted, record counts, solver calls and maximum absolute,
weighted and rule-residual adjustments. `per_sweep` retains the corresponding
sweep summaries. Records counted as already satisfying were never adjusted
in any sweep. With `m > 1`, the attribute is a list of summaries by imputation.

Saving optimization problems is optional; otherwise no solver structures or
original stochastic prediction vectors are retained. Saved problems are grouped
by sweep and include feasible predictions with a NULL solver input, as well as
record indices, variable names, weights, constraint matrices, original
predictions, adjusted values, ECOS inputs/output/status and residuals.
`stochastic_predictions` preserves all eligible numeric cells of that record
before projection, including cells outside the active edits.
`restricted_optimization_problems` remains a separate attribute.

```{r diagnostics}
attr(result, "edit_diagnostics")
attr(result, "edit_optimization_problems")[[1]][[1]]
attr(result, "restricted_optimization_problems")
```

## Supported edits and limitations

Supported edits are record-wise linear bounds, equalities and inequalities,
including coefficients determined by fixed values. For example,
`amount <= fixed_rate * observed_total` is linear after substitution.
Conditions must depend only on fixed values. Disjunctions are supported when
one alternative is determined from fixed values, such as
`industry == "A" | amount >= 0`. A conditional consequence can contain
several jointly applied edits. Strict inequalities use an interior margin of
twice the absolute tolerance.

The continuous optimizer rejects adjustable integer columns, nonlinear edits,
conditions depending on adjustable values, and unresolved nonconvex or
mixed-integer disjunctions. Cross-record or aggregate constraints are not
supported. Use continuous numeric storage only when fractional values are
meaningful. Infeasibility or numerical failure raises `vimpute_edit_error`,
with the record and rule names available on the error condition. No policy for
silently retaining invalid predictions is provided.

Formula convenience wrappers apply the same projector jointly after assembling
their LHS columns. Their RHS missings remain outside projection eligibility.
`tabiclImpute()` forwards edit arguments directly to `vimpute()`.
